purpose: To support arts and culture in Manitoba through funding the creation and sharing of art by Manitoba artists.
improve: Speaking as an artist working primarily in theatre, the arts community would be much better supported if a significant amount of funding was shifted out of Operating and into Create and Present funding. It seems completely lopsided, for example, for RMTC as a single organization with a large donor base to receive over $100,000 more than all individual artists and groups in the province receive in Create funding annually. As costs go up, organizations receiving operating funding are leaning more and more on individual artists to fund creation, research, and development, while receiving almost 10x the provincial funding available to those individual artists. I strongly believe that arts and culture in Manitoba would be significantly improved and made more sustainable by a restructuring of funding that more equitably supported the individual artists who actually create the work these larger organizations present. I believe that, were more funding allocated to individual artists, there would me more art made and shared in the province, that work would be more diverse and more accessible to audiences, and Manitoba would, over time, see a higher national and international profile as a hub of arts and culture.
future_impact_txt: I believe that MAC could have a more significant impact on the arts and cultural community by redirecting funds from operating grants for large organizations into individual artists and small artist run centres. MAC also has the power to hold large organizations accountable to their communities by requiring more equitable practices in order to maintain Operating funding. That, for example, the RWB has maintained such a large amount of provincial funding through their many failures to provide safe working conditions and the resignation of their Indigenous advisory board shows a lack of accountability to the community that public funding should uphold. I hope that in 10 years Manitoba will have a stronger, healthier arts community where artists are able to make a living wage year round.
comments_txt: I appreciate all of MAC's work so much, I am so thankful to have such an honest, open, generous, and forward thinking staff to communicate with.

purpose: To fund the development and dissemination of artistic practices, projects, and organizations in Manitoba
improve: A disproportionate amount of money feels like it is going to large arts organizations that employ large numbers of salaried administrators (including dedicated fundraising and patron staff) while simultaneously undercutting freelance artists through unfair contract negotiations and limited contract work. I think this really limits both the feasibility of freelance artists to have a career, as well as the public's perception of what "art" in Manitoba could mean. It feels like there are brief glimmers--an extraordinary ARC gallery show, a self-produced experimental theatre show, a night like Nuit Blanche--where a future of work that embraces imagination, diversity of practice, and 'non-commercial' aesthetics feels possible in Manitoba, and I just wish it felt like that year-round. I wish independent artists were better resourced to make their careers, livelihoods, and artistic visions a reality. Large arts organizations have access to resources in terms of funding streams independent artists simply don't--including one-off federal cash infusions as we've seen in the prairies over the last couple of years. Concretely, I wish that less council money went to these organizations, and more money went, specifically, towards Explore and Create, and Present grants, as I believe these are the MAC programs that are best suited to supporting artists in their day-to-day practices and lives, as well as the broader Manitoba public's experience of art in our province.
future_impact_txt: Successfully advocated for increases in provincial funding--as well as changes to internal financial allocations--that significantly improve the amount of resources independent artists receive. Ultimately I believe that independent artists are the heartbeat of what makes culture local, vibrant, and communal--large arts organizations are at their best when they are following the lead of artists. In 10 years time, I hope that MAC's work has become more aligned with this reality.

purpose: Provides funding for the creation and sharing of arts and culture for the benefit of all Manitobans
improve:
I’d love to see more micro-grants that are truly accessible, and a larger percentage of overall funding directed toward small and mid-sized artists and companies.

This year, only 25% of Create grants were funded, which shows the need for a higher budget in that category. 

Meanwhile, operating funds for the RWB, WSO, and MTC were each around $800,000—equal to the total funding for all Create grants combined. That doesn’t feel equitable.

I understand these are different funding streams and that large institutions also need support, but I believe more, smaller grants for independent and emerging artists would strengthen Manitoba’s arts ecosystem far more.

After all, how can a small company compete with an organization that can afford a professional grant writer?

(I would also like to choose something between connected and disconnected in question number 10, but it's not an option).
future_impact_txt:
MAC’s funding is focused where it makes the greatest impact—investing in small and mid-sized artists and companies whose creative work truly shapes Manitoba’s cultural landscape but who lack access to the same private and corporate resources as larger institutions.  

There is more equity between the total funding toward create, share, tour of individual artists and small companies and the funding toward any one large professional arts organization.

These artists and organizations are often the ones creating new work, filling gaps in Manitoba’s arts scene, and bringing forward fresh voices and visions. Supporting them not only fosters innovation but ensures a more diverse and vibrant arts community across the province.

MAC also has the unique ability to provide early-stage support and credibility—the kind of seed funding that helps emerging organizations grow to a point where they can attract additional partners, sponsors, and private funding.

By focusing more of its resources in this direction, MAC could help build a more balanced and equitable arts ecosystem, rather than one where smaller companies must compete against institutions with professional grant writers and dedicated fundraising teams.
comments_txt:
I believe MAC should reassess its priorities in light of the reality that private donations, corporate sponsorships, and foundation grants already tend to flow toward larger institutions. 

Perhaps MAC could even play a role in connecting smaller companies to those private opportunities, while using its public funds to nurture the growth of new art and emerging voices in Manitoba.

Ten years from now, the Manitoba Arts Council has reshaped the arts and cultural landscape by investing in sustainability, shared infrastructure, and equitable access for artists and organizations.

Through bold policy changes and innovative funding models, arts organizations that do not own their buildings now have the opportunity to purchase and share creative spaces, fostering long-term stability. For individual artists, MAC’s funding programs have evolved to provide three annual opportunities to apply for project, creation, and career development support. This has fostered consistency and financial security for artists, allowing them to plan their creative work over longer timelines.

purpose: The goal should be to ensure that all Manitobans have access to the arts. However, current funding is heavily weighted toward supporting the arts in Winnipeg. This imbalance has been longstanding and needs to be corrected. There are many rural and northern communities that lack access to the arts, and addressing this gap should be a key focus moving forward.
improve:
We need to restore balance and increase arts funding for rural and northern Manitoba. Funding should be more reflective of the population—at least 40% of Manitobans live in rural areas. This doesn’t even include artists working in schools.

Winnipeg has the Winnipeg Arts Council (WAC), which provides additional funding for the arts, but rural and northern regions rely solely on the Manitoba Arts Council (MAC) as their core funder. When responsibility for arts funding was transferred from the province to MAC, rural funding actually decreased because new limits were introduced that prevented many rural organizations from applying for project grants.

$30,000 doesn’t even cover the cost of one staff position—it’s an abysmal level of support.
disconnect_explain_txt: MAC is more connected to Winnipeg artists, but there is a clear disconnect when it comes to rural and northern arts and their unique needs to thrive. The arts in these regions operate on an entirely different level, with distinct challenges and contexts that require more tailored support.
future_impact_txt:
Ten years from now, the arts will be thriving in every rural and northern community across Manitoba. Municipalities will recognize the social and economic impact of the arts and will be actively investing in them, creating more vibrant, connected, and engaged communities.

This progress will be the direct result of MAC’s commitment to increased investment in rural and northern arts and its success in securing matching funding to amplify that impact.

A province-wide school touring program will bring performing arts to students throughout Manitoba, inspiring creativity and nurturing the next generation of artists and audiences.

Manitobans of all ages will participate in and experience the arts as a natural and essential part of everyday life—because the arts will truly belong to everyone, everywhere.
comments_txt:
The current system is unsustainable and lopsided, with most funding, infrastructure, and opportunities concentrated in Winnipeg. Meanwhile, rural and Northern communities—home to approximately 40% of Manitoba’s population—remain under-resourced, underserved, and often excluded from decision-making and investment.

There are at least 14 long-standing, volunteer-driven arts organizations operating in rural Manitoba today. Many have served their communities for decades, but are now nearing burnout. Without renewed investment and structural support, these organizations—and the ecosystems they anchor—risk disappearing altogether. If we don’t strengthen rural arts staffing and infrastructure now, it will recede rapidly, and the cultural gap between urban and rural Manitoba will only widen.
 
This is not about potential—it’s about what’s already proven possible. There are currently four NHL players who were born and raised in rural Manitoba. That’s possible because nearly every rural municipality has a hockey rink. Now imagine what the arts could look like if every rural community had access to an arts centre and vibrant arts programming.
 
These challenges point to the need for equity-focused funding. Rural and Northern organizations often lack the administrative capacity to compete with large, urban institutions, and without a new approach, future funding risks reinforcing privilege and systemic barriers rather than reducing them.
 
To address these issues holistically, I strongly recommend that the Manitoba Arts Council and the Winnipeg Foundation commission a province-wide arts ecosystem review. This review should guide not only the design of this new grant program but also inform long-term planning across the sector.
 
Below are six core recommendations that support this vision.
 
1. Commission a Provincial Arts Ecosystem Review
Hire an independent consultant to assess the health of Manitoba’s arts and culture ecosystem and provide actionable recommendations. The review should include:
Identifying opportunities for collaboration, amalgamation, or shared services
Evaluating the capacity and utilization of existing venues and touring networks
Mapping regional disparities and barriers to participation
Proposing a strategic framework for funding distribution
The resulting report could serve as a guiding document for both funders and policymakers, including the development of an updated provincial Cultural Plan. Organizations like the Manitoba Benefactors for the Arts may be interested in supporting this initiative.

2. Fund Sustainability, Not Expansion Alone
The goal of this new program must be to foster a sustainable and inclusive arts ecosystem, not just to fund more activity or capital projects. Manitoba’s current model is top-heavy, and rural and Northern communities have significant untapped potential that will remain unrealized without targeted investment.

3. Prioritize Equity in Funding Distribution
Equity requires more than an open call. I recommend that 40% of the program’s total funding be earmarked for rural, Northern, and Indigenous-led organizations. This formula should be applied consistently by both MAC and the Winnipeg Foundation, recognizing the demographic and geographic realities of the province.

4. Avoid Overconcentration in Winnipeg
Winnipeg’s arts sector is already saturated with organizations, venues, and existing funding streams. Future funds should prioritize diverse voices and geographic inclusion, not duplicate services in already well-resourced areas.

5. Prevent Fragmentation and Support Impact
The current proliferation of small, niche organizations—each competing for limited resources—is weakening the ecosystem. Funding should encourage collaboration and shared infrastructure to maximize collective impact and reduce duplication.

6. Learn from Other Sector Models
Sectors such as Sport Manitoba offer effective frameworks for regional investment, sustainability, and oversight. The arts sector could benefit from adopting similar checks and balances, ensuring long-term viability and fairness across Manitoba.

We are not traditional presenters, we build tours working with either community volunteers are partner organization to host low overhead , and intimate concerts for Artists from Manitoba , Canada and beyond to perform in Rural and urban communities in Manitoba and the rest of Canada.
purpose: To fund Arts organizations and their endeavors in the province, and in a limited way, support artists ( musicians)
improve:
One of the most significant barriers we face is the requirement to report through CADAC. This system does not reflect the reality of how many community-based and touring organizations actually operate. Our model is unique but effective: we design, schedule, promote, and deliver concerts; we guarantee artists fair fees; we pay artists immediately at the venue through ticket revenue collected by local volunteers; and we reconcile our share only after the performances. This model ensures artists are paid quickly and fairly while keeping our administrative costs low and community impact high.

However, CADAC only allows us to report a fraction of our actual activity and revenue—only revenue that goes through our bank account, which is 20% of the income directly generated through our work. As a result, our organization appears artificially small and underperforming on paper, despite running 18 successful seasons of province-wide cultural service. This creates a distorted view that negatively affects assessment, funding levels, and credibility. We have explained this repeatedly, yet there has been no meaningful adjustment to accommodate organizations like ours.

The current system seems designed for large urban institutions with conventional box-office models—not flexible, grassroots cultural networks that prioritize access, affordability, and artist-centred economics. If the Arts Council truly values diversity in the cultural ecosystem, it must adopt funding and reporting systems that recognize different, equally valid models of success.

In addition, the ongoing burden of excessive reporting and justification is draining valuable time and resources. Legacy organizations with decades of proven impact should not be forced to repeatedly re-prove our worth. There should be a tiered trust system and streamlined reporting for organizations with sustained track records and demonstrated community value. Accountability is important, but it must be balanced with respect for organizational capacity and recognition of long-term contribution.

In short:
	•	Replace or significantly reform CADAC so it accurately captures diverse revenue and operational models.
	•	Introduce flexible reporting frameworks for organizations delivering community impact in non-traditional ways.
	•	Reduce administrative burden for long-standing, mission-driven organizations so we can focus on delivering cultural programming—not paperwork.

The Arts Council has an opportunity to become a true partner in building cultural infrastructure rather than a gatekeeper of outdated systems.
future_impact_txt:
In ten years, I hope to see the Arts Council…

A visible and vocal champion for the arts—one that actively advocates for significantly increased public investment in artists and cultural organizations. The arts should be impossible to overlook, even for those who aren’t already paying attention.

I envision an Arts Council that treats organizations of all sizes—with different mandates, histories, and community impacts—with equal respect. In the past, important cultural initiatives like the Folk Festival, the West End Cultural Centre and Home Routes struggled for recognition and support. It shouldn’t take years of persistence or political restructuring for innovative, community-driven ideas to be valued.

The Arts Council of the future will remove unnecessary barriers for new and emerging organizations. It will recognize that meaningful cultural work doesn’t always fit inside rigid eligibility criteria, competitive silos, or one-size-fits-all funding portals. Flexibility must be built into the system, because creative ecosystems thrive on experimentation and community entrepreneurship.

I would also like to see a shift in priorities—less bureaucracy and institutional overhead, and more funding reaching artists and organizations on the ground. Community arts groups are the cultural fabric of this province. Many of us operate with modest budgets, paying living wages where we can, and generating cultural and social impact far beyond our financial size. Yet we still struggle to grow sustainably. Every dollar should reflect the value and necessity of what we contribute.

In short: less red tape, more trust. Less gatekeeping, more partnership. Less performative administration, and more investment where it matters—in artists, creativity, and community. That’s the Arts Council we hope to work with in the next decade.
comments_txt:
We are genuinely grateful for the support we receive and for the work the Arts Council does for the cultural sector. We especially want to acknowledge Cathleen Enns, whose understanding of our work and consistent advocacy have made a real difference. She is thoughtful, responsive, and committed to helping us navigate challenges, and we deeply value her partnership.

Thank you for the opportunity to share our perspective—we care about this relationship and look forward to continuing to build something meaningful for artists and communities together.

MAC has become too political, clearly prioritizing ideology ahead of artistic impact and ability. The average Manitoban does not seem them reflected in a lot of the programming or organizations you fund, leaving them disconnected from our incredible arts and cultural sector. 

Be impactful, not performative.
